paper_metadata.title: NExt ApplicationS of Quantum Computing - D5.7: Update of review of state-of-the-art for Pricing and Computation of VaR

summary: This report reviews gate-based quantum finance methods for pricing and VaR, centered on quantum accelerated Monte Carlo and amplitude estimation. The paper gives asymptotic AE query scalings such as O(1/epsilon_a) versus classical Monte Carlo O(1/epsilon_a^2), but the experimental evidence remains small-scale and noise-limited; for PDE-based pricing, the authors note that high-dimensional amplitude readout can erase the potential advantage. In the state-preparation section, one cited variational experiment used 2 qubits with 15 gates, and another QFT-based loading study reported only qualitative results on Quantinuum H1-1/H1-2.

experiments.description: Quantum state preparation / probability distribution loading for financial Monte Carlo and pricing, including methods such as quantum binomial tree, Grover-Rudolph-style loading, low-rank state preparation, decision-diagram loading, variational loading, MPS-based loading, QFT-based loading, and related initialization techniques reviewed in the report.

algorithm.variant: state preparation / initialization methods for QAMC

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Load probability distributions or payoff functions into amplitudes of an n-qubit register; in some methods the vector is encoded over 2^n basis states, with variants using binary-encoded states, unitary encoding, or function loading.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Prepare |f> or |v> such that amplitudes encode a target probability distribution or function values for downstream pricing / VaR algorithms.

problem_instance.description: Review of multiple state-preparation methods applied to financial distributions and option-pricing inputs; examples include normal distributions, Black-Scholes distributions, European call option, and generic payoff / PDF loading.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Varies by cited work; reported examples include simulator studies, noisy-QPU experiments, and hardware demonstrations on Quantinuum devices.

speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical Monte Carlo / classical state preparation
speedup_claims.conditions: General QAMC motivation; not demonstrated as a unified benchmark for the state-preparation papers
speedup_claims.caveats: The report emphasizes that no initialization method satisfies all requirements simultaneously; many methods require too many qubits or too much depth for NISQ hardware.

speedup_claims.conditions: For the Zhang et al. 2022 method; circuit depth scaling
speedup_claims.caveats: Total gate count still scales as O(2^n).

speedup_claims.factor: less than 13% of Grover-Rudolph gate count
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a gate-count reduction for a specific approximate loading method, not a general speedup guarantee.

speedup_claims.conditions: Mixed top-down/bottom-up tree traversal with midpoint s = log2(N)/2
speedup_claims.caveats: Requires additional auxiliary qubits and produces entangled states in some variants.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Varies by method; examples in the report include O(n), O(2^n), O(kn), sublinear depth/width, or polynomial-depth approximations depending on the state-preparation technique.
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Not uniformly specified; often exponential classical preprocessing for exact loading or polynomial for approximate/sparse cases.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: No unified benchmark; many methods require O(2^n) gates or substantial auxiliary qubits, and the report emphasizes NISQ infeasibility.
limiting_factors: often exponential classical preprocessing for exact loading
no single experimental benchmark across methods

notes: This is a synthesis of multiple reviewed state-preparation papers rather than one single experiment; the report gives qualitative or asymptotic resource statements for each cited method, but not a unified experimental benchmark.
Section 3.1 is a survey of state-preparation methods, not a single performance demonstration.
The paper explicitly notes that none of the methods satisfy all requirements and that many are impractical on current processors.

experiments.description: Amplitude estimation experiments and benchmarks for financial pricing / VaR, including noisy and hardware demonstrations of MLAE, IQAE, FAE, AdaptQAE, RQAE, and related variants.

algorithm.variant: MLAE / IQAE / FAE / AdaptQAE / RQAE family of amplitude estimation methods

hyperparameters.schedule: linear / exponential / adaptive / random-depth / modified Grover variants depending on cited work

problem_formulation.encoding_details: A financial quantity is encoded as amplitude a in a state |Psi> = A|0>^n = sqrt(a)|psi1> + sqrt(1-a)|psi0>; the oracle A is built from state preparation plus payoff encoding.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate amplitude a corresponding to a pricing or risk quantity with precision epsilon_a and confidence 1-delta.

problem_instance.description: Financial amplitude-estimation tasks for pricing and VaR; the report references credit risk, option pricing, and generic Monte Carlo acceleration settings.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Benchmarks and simulations across multiple cited works; some experiments on IBM superconducting devices and Honeywell/Quantinuum trapped-ion devices, with comparisons to Monte Carlo and noise models.

noise_model.noise_type: depolarising / dephasing / amplitude damping / Gaussian phase noise depending on cited work
noise_model.error_mitigation_method: noise-aware modeling, randomized compiling, depth jittering, modified schedules, and parameter orthogonalization in cited studies

implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Classical aggregation / maximum-likelihood / Bayesian inference / confidence-interval updates depending on the AE variant.

speedup_claims.caveats: The report notes that practical noise and depth constraints often prevent achieving the ideal quadratic speedup.

speedup_claims.conditions: AdaptiveQAE experiments reported in the cited work
speedup_claims.caveats: The report also states that the number of oracle calls can be slightly higher than in IQAE/MLAE despite the runtime improvement.

speedup_claims.conditions: Faster Amplitude Estimation (FAE) as claimed by Nakaji (2020)
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a claim summarized in the report; no unified financial benchmark is provided.

speedup_claims.factor: quadratic speedup not achievable under tested noise
speedup_claims.conditions: MLAE under depolarising, dephasing, and amplitude damping noise in simulations
speedup_claims.caveats: The report says even low-strength noise can destroy the quadratic advantage for exponential schedules.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Typically O(1/epsilon_a) or better for AE variants; the report tabulates asymptotic query complexity for several algorithms.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: toy to small problem sizes only
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Low-depth AE variants can reduce query counts toward O(1/epsilon_a), but the paper reports noise-limited performance and no practical end-to-end advantage.
limiting_factors: quadratic speedup not realized in practice

notes: The report explicitly mentions experiments on IBM quantum computers and Honeywell/Quantinuum H1 trapped-ion devices for some AE studies, but it does not provide a single unified hardware configuration for all AE variants.
The paper tabulates asymptotic query complexity improvements for AE, but the experimental sections report that noise and depth prevent practical quadratic speedup.
Hardware experiments are on IBM superconducting devices and Honeywell/Quantinuum trapped-ion devices, but only for small-scale demonstrations.

experiments.description: Quantum algorithms for solving pricing PDEs, including imaginary-time evolution / variational Hilbert-space evolution and finite-difference-based quantum linear differential equation solvers for multi-asset derivatives.

algorithm.variant: imaginary-time evolution / variational Hilbert space evolution; quantum algorithm for linear differential equations

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Encode initial condition or discretized PDE state into a quantum state; evolve under a Hamiltonian or solve a discretized ODE system arising from finite differences.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Compute derivative prices by evolving the pricing PDE or its discretized form and extracting the relevant expectation / amplitude.
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: Hermitian Hamiltonian corresponding to the Wick-rotated pricing PDE / Black-Scholes-type operator

problem_instance.description: European vanilla call option; multi-asset barrier option; double knock-out barrier option on a single asset.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Numerical results and complexity estimates; one cited work computes Toffoli-gate complexity for a particular example, another demonstrates a small-device variational implementation.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Finite-difference discretization of the PDE; in the variational version, embedding of the probability distribution and SWAP-test-based inner product estimation.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Recover option price from evolved state / expectation value.

speedup_claims.conditions: Finite-difference quantum method for high-dimensional pricing PDEs
speedup_claims.caveats: The report states the complexity as poly(epsilon^-1, d) and notes that the method is analyzed in terms of Toffoli gates for a particular example.

speedup_claims.factor: potentially exponential vs polynomial in dimension
speedup_claims.baseline_method: naive grid-based extraction / classical high-dimensional discretization
speedup_claims.caveats: The report warns that reading out amplitudes can destroy the advantage if done naively.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Reported as poly(epsilon^-1, d) for the finite-difference quantum method, and O(poly(d log(epsilon^-1))) for the variational small-device version.
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Exponential in dimension for naive grid-based extraction; finite-difference classical methods are the baseline.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Potential polynomial improvement in the finite-difference / ODE formulation is discussed, but extraction of the price from amplitudes remains costly.
limiting_factors: amplitude readout bottleneck in high dimensions

notes: The report states that the variational PDE approach can be implemented on a small quantum computer and that the finite-difference method is analyzed in terms of Toffoli gates, but it does not give a single consolidated qubit count or depth for all PDE experiments.
Section 4 gives algorithmic proposals and complexity expressions, but no clear experimental quantum-vs-classical advantage is demonstrated.
The paper explicitly notes that direct amplitude extraction in high dimensions loses the potential quantum advantage.

experiments.description: Quantum reinforcement learning / deep hedging experiment for portfolio hedging in finance using a trapped-ion processor.

algorithm.variant: quantum reinforcement learning for deep hedging; distributional actor-critic with orthogonal and compound layers

problem_formulation.encoding_details: One qubit per time step to simulate asset-price evolution in a rough Geometric Brownian Motion approximation.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Learn a hedging policy / actor-critic policy for deep hedging under transaction costs and related constraints.

problem_instance.description: Deep hedging / portfolio hedging under transaction costs; rough GBM approximation of asset-price evolution.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Comparison against classical and alternative quantum approaches; performance and parameter-count reduction reported qualitatively.

speedup_claims.conditions: Quantum reinforcement learning for deep hedging on a trapped-ion processor
speedup_claims.caveats: The report says the quantum implementation reduces the number of trained parameters and provides better performance than alternative classical and quantum alternatives, but no quantitative benchmark is given in the excerpt.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Not specified beyond circuit-based implementation with up to 16 qubits.

notes: The report explicitly says a trapped-ion quantum processor was used and circuits with up to 16 qubits were considered, but it does not provide depth, gate counts, or optimizer details.

experiments.description: Quantum computational finance experiments for pricing derivatives via quantum zero-sum game, quantum simplex, and quantum pseudoinverse methods in incomplete markets / single-period market settings.

algorithm.variant: quantum zero-sum game algorithm; quantum simplex; quantum pseudoinverse / linear-systems approach

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Assumes quantum access to asset prices and payoff matrix in a single-period market; risk-neutral pricing is posed as a linear program or least-square market problem.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Compute arbitrage-free derivative price / martingale risk-neutral measure / pseudoinverse-based valuation.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Linear-program constraints; regularization in the Black-Scholes call-option example.

problem_instance.description: Black-Scholes call options; incomplete-market pricing; single-period market valuation.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: The report summarizes theoretical algorithms and mentions comparison between quantum zero-sum game and quantum simplex in an appendix; no unified hardware benchmark is given in the report text.

speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical linear programming / simplex / pseudoinverse methods
speedup_claims.conditions: Quantum zero-sum game, quantum simplex, and quantum pseudoinverse approaches for incomplete markets
speedup_claims.caveats: The report provides only a high-level summary and does not include numerical benchmark results in the excerpt.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Not specified in the report beyond claims of speedup for the quantum subroutines.

notes: The report discusses these as algorithmic proposals and does not provide a concrete experimental hardware setup in the text excerpt.

experiments.description: Quantum binomial tree state-preparation method for derivative pricing.
key_results: Presented in Section 3.1 as a finance-specific initialization method.
Probability loading is described as efficient, but the number of required gates is too large for NISQ-era implementation.
Gaussian steps are approximated by a discrete distribution with only two values, yielding a coarse approximation.

experiments.description: Split Step Quantum Walk (SSQW) method for loading probability distributions / real-valued amplitudes, applied to European call option pricing.

algorithm.variant: Split Step Quantum Walk with variational parameter selection

key_results: Section 3.1 reports application to the European call option.
Achieved a reasonable result with only 5 qubits and in less than 20 seconds.

experiments.description: Quantum Fourier Transform-based function loading for periodic and non-periodic functions, with experiments on Quantinuum H1-1 and H1-2.
key_results: Section 3.1 states that experiments on Quantinuum H1-1 and H1-2 quantum computers gave qualitatively good results.
The paper does not provide a quantitative metric, only a qualitative comparison / figure.

experiments.description: Variational quantum state-preparation experiments using reinforcement learning, genetic algorithms, qGANs, and related methods for loading distributions.

algorithm.variant: variational state preparation / qGAN / genetic algorithm loading
algorithm.optimizer: reinforcement learning / genetic algorithm / qGAN training

key_results: Section 3.1 reports a simulator experiment on 2 qubits with fidelity described as modest and minimum gate count of 15.
Other cited works report noisy-QPU fidelities that remain far from requirements and degrade quickly with qubit count.
